title: rails/rails: Issues containing 'ActiveJob Job'
description: rails/rails: Issues containing 'ActiveJob Job' on GitHub

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

By the time an ActiveJob::Base#perform method is invoked, Active
Record instances are already deserialized and reified through GlobalID
integration.

For example, consider the following model and job classes:

class ApplicationRecord < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.strict_loading_by_default = true
end

class Article < ApplicationRecord
  has_and_belongs_to_many :tags
end

class Tag < ApplicationRecord
  has_and_belongs_to_many :articles
end

class PublishJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(article)
    article.tags.each do |tag|
      # ...
    end
  end
end

Since application code does not have an opportunity to configure
anything about that loading process (including which associations are
eagerly loaded), it's common for Active Job executions to raise Active
Record strict loading errors:

ActiveRecord::StrictLoadingViolationError: `Article` is marked for strict_loading. The Tag association named `:tags` cannot be lazily loaded.

Detail

The GlobalID::Locator.locate interface supports optional keyword
options that configure how to query Active Record during the location
process. For example, the includes: keyword argument is transformed
into a call to includes while constructing the Active Record query.

This commit introduces the ActiveJob::Base.locator_options method to
configure how each test class wants to load records deserialized from
GlobalID values.

class PublishJob < ApplicationJob
+  locator_options "Article", includes: :tags
+
   def perform(article)
     article.tags.each do |tag|
       # ...
     end
   end
 end

The first argument is a class name (in the style of the Active Record
:class_name option for associations), and subsequent keyword options
are forwarded to GlobalID::Locator.locate.

Checklist

Before submitting the PR make sure the following are checked:

  • This Pull Request is related to one change. Changes that are unrelated should be opened in separate PRs.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: [Fix #issue-number]
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.
items.title: Introduce `ActiveJob::Base.locator_options`

items.content_html:
Steps to reproduce

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
  # If you want to test against edge Rails replace the previous line with this:
  # gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "active_job/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"
  config.active_job.queue_adapter = :test

  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
  end
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
end

class LoopingJob < ActiveJob::Base
  self.enqueue_after_transaction_commit = true

  def perform
    Post.transaction do
      retry_job wait: 5.second
    end
  end
end

class LoopingJobTest < ActiveJob::TestCase
  def test_stuff
    LoopingJob.perform_now
    
    scheduled = enqueued_jobs.last["scheduled_at"]

    assert_not_nil scheduled
  end
end

Expected behavior

The job should be scheduled 5 seconds in the future

Actual behavior

The job has no scheduled_at, meaning its enqueued immediately

System configuration

Rails version: 8.1.3 (#55141 broke this)

Ruby version: N/A

items.content_html:
Steps to reproduce

In a Rails 8.1 app using Puma + Solid Queue (in-process mode via solid_queue.connects_to), BroadcastLogger formatters lose their TaggedLogging::Formatter extensions after Solid Queue forks worker processes. This causes a NoMethodError when any code path calls logger.tagged(...).

Setup that triggers this in production:

# config/environments/production.rb
config.log_tags = [:request_id]
config.active_job.queue_adapter = :solid_queue
config.solid_queue.connects_to = { database: { writing: :queue } }

The default production logger in Rails 8.1 is a BroadcastLogger wrapping a TaggedLogging logger. The TaggedLogging module extends the formatter with TaggedLogging::Formatter, which adds #current_tags and #tagged.

Reproduction path in production:

  1. Puma boots and Rails creates the logger. Rails.logger is a BroadcastLogger whose broadcasts have formatters with TaggedLogging::Formatter extensions.
  2. Puma forks worker processes.
  3. Solid Queue starts in-process within the Puma worker.
  4. After the fork, the formatter on one or more broadcast loggers loses its TaggedLogging::Formatter extensions and becomes a plain Proc or Logger::SimpleFormatter.
  5. An ActiveJob runs and ActiveJob::Logging#tag_logger calls logger.tagged("ActiveJob", ...).
  6. TaggedLogging#tagged (line 141) delegates to formatter.tagged(...).
  7. The formatter is a Proc which doesn't respond to #tagged.
  8. NoMethodError: undefined method 'tagged' for an instance of Proc

The same crash occurs when ActionCable broadcasts during a job (e.g., Turbo Streams), because ActionCable's logger (ActionCable.server.logger) references the same corrupted BroadcastLogger.

Executable reproduction script:

# frozen_string_literal: true

# Reproduction: BroadcastLogger + TaggedLogging formatter corruption after fork.
# Run with: ruby reproduction.rb

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"
  gem "rails", "~> 8.1"
end

require "active_support"
require "active_support/broadcast_logger"
require "active_support/tagged_logging"
require "active_job"
require "logger"

puts "Rails #{Rails.gem_version}, Ruby #{RUBY_VERSION}"
puts

# Create a logger the way Rails production does
inner_logger = ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging.logger(STDOUT)
logger = ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger.new(inner_logger)

puts "=== Before fork ==="
fmt = logger.broadcasts.first.formatter
puts "Formatter class: #{fmt.class}"
puts "Responds to :tagged? #{fmt.respond_to?(:tagged)}"
puts "Responds to :current_tags? #{fmt.respond_to?(:current_tags)}"
logger.tagged("BeforeFork") { logger.info "This works" }
puts

# Simulate the formatter corruption that happens after Puma -> Solid Queue fork.
# In production, the formatter loses its TaggedLogging::Formatter extensions and
# reverts to a plain Proc. We simulate this directly:
puts "=== Simulating post-fork formatter corruption ==="
logger.broadcasts.first.formatter = proc { |severity, time, progname, msg| "#{msg}\n" }
fmt = logger.broadcasts.first.formatter
puts "Formatter class: #{fmt.class}"
puts "Responds to :tagged? #{fmt.respond_to?(:tagged)}"
puts

# Crash point 1: TaggedLogging#tagged delegates to formatter.tagged(...)
puts "=== Crash point 1: logger.tagged ==="
begin
  logger.tagged("ActiveJob") { logger.info "This should work" }
  puts "OK"
rescue NoMethodError => e
  puts "CRASHED: #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
end
puts

# Crash point 2: ActiveJob::Logging#logger_tagged_by_active_job? calls formatter.current_tags
puts "=== Crash point 2: formatter.current_tags ==="
begin
  logger.formatter.current_tags
  puts "OK"
rescue NoMethodError => e
  puts "CRASHED: #{e.class}: #{e.message}"
end
puts

# Real fork test — demonstrates formatter corruption survives fork
puts "=== Real fork test ==="
read_io, write_io = IO.pipe
pid = fork do
  read_io.close
  fmt = logger.broadcasts.first.formatter
  write_io.puts "Formatter responds to :tagged after fork? #{fmt.respond_to?(:tagged)} (class: #{fmt.class})"
  begin
    logger.tagged("ForkedProcess") { logger.info "test" }
    write_io.puts "tagged call: OK"
  rescue NoMethodError => e
    write_io.puts "tagged call: CRASHED - #{e.message}"
  end
  write_io.close
end
write_io.close
Process.wait(pid)
puts read_io.read
read_io.close

Output:

Rails 8.1.3, Ruby 4.0.1

=== Before fork ===
Formatter class: ActiveSupport::Logger::SimpleFormatter
Responds to :tagged? true
Responds to :current_tags? true
[BeforeFork] This works

=== Simulating post-fork formatter corruption ===
Formatter class: Proc
Responds to :tagged? false

=== Crash point 1: logger.tagged ===
CRASHED: NoMethodError: undefined method 'tagged' for an instance of Proc

=== Crash point 2: formatter.current_tags ===
CRASHED: NoMethodError: undefined method 'current_tags' for an instance of Proc

=== Real fork test ===
Formatter responds to :tagged after fork? false (class: Proc)
tagged call: CRASHED - undefined method 'tagged' for an instance of Proc

Expected behavior

BroadcastLogger should preserve TaggedLogging::Formatter extensions on its broadcast formatters across process forks. Calling logger.tagged(...) should work regardless of whether the process has forked.

At a minimum, TaggedLogging#tagged and ActiveJob::Logging#logger_tagged_by_active_job? should guard against formatters that don't respond to #tagged / #current_tags rather than crashing with NoMethodError.

Actual behavior

After a Puma -> Solid Queue fork, BroadcastLogger broadcast formatters lose their TaggedLogging::Formatter extensions. The formatter reverts to a plain Proc, and any call to logger.tagged(...) raises:

NoMethodError: undefined method 'tagged' for an instance of Proc

Full stack trace from production:

/activesupport-8.1.3/lib/active_support/tagged_logging.rb:143:in 'ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging#tagged'
/activesupport-8.1.3/lib/active_support/broadcast_logger.rb:228:in 'ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger#method_missing'
/activejob-8.1.3/lib/active_job/logging.rb:39:in 'ActiveJob::Logging#tag_logger'
/activejob-8.1.3/lib/active_job/logging.rb:32:in 'ActiveJob::Logging#perform_now'
/activejob-8.1.3/lib/active_job/execution_state.rb:7:in 'block (2 levels) in ActiveJob::ExecutionState#perform_now'
/activesupport-8.1.3/core_ext/time/zones.rb:65:in 'Time.use_zone'
/activejob-8.1.3/lib/active_job/execution_state.rb:7:in 'block in ActiveJob::ExecutionState#perform_now'
/i18n-1.14.8/lib/i18n.rb:349:in 'I18n::Base.with_locale'
/activejob-8.1.3/lib/active_job/execution_state.rb:6:in 'ActiveJob::ExecutionState#perform_now'
/activejob-8.1.3/lib/active_job/execution.rb:23:in 'ActiveJob::Execution::ClassMethods#perform_now'
/solid_cable-3.0.12/lib/action_cable/subscription_adapter/solid_cable.rb:21:in ...
/actioncable-8.1.3/lib/action_cable/subscription_adapter/channel_prefix.rb:10:in ...
/actioncable-8.1.3/lib/action_cable/server/broadcasting.rb:58:in ...
/activesupport-8.1.3/lib/active_support/notifications.rb:212:in ...
/actioncable-8.1.3/lib/action_cable/server/broadcasting.rb:56:in ...
/actioncable-8.1.3/lib/action_cable/server/broadcasting.rb:34:in ...
/turbo-rails-2.0.23/app/channels/turbo/streams/broadcasts.rb:103:in ...

Root cause analysis

The issue is in the interaction between BroadcastLogger, TaggedLogging, and process forking:

  1. TaggedLogging::Formatter is mixed in via extend (source). The formatter object gets singleton methods like #tagged and #current_tags at runtime.

  2. After a fork, these singleton method extensions can be lost. The formatter object survives the fork, but its singleton class may not carry over the extended module's methods correctly. In our case, the formatter becomes a plain Proc.

  3. TaggedLogging#tagged (line 141-143) calls formatter.tagged(...) without checking whether the formatter actually responds to #tagged:

    def tagged(*tags)
  if block_given?
    formatter.tagged(*tags) { yield self }  # <-- crashes here
  # ...

  4. ActiveJob::Logging#logger_tagged_by_active_job? (line 45-47) calls logger.formatter.current_tags without checking if the formatter responds to it:

    def logger_tagged_by_active_job?
  logger.formatter.current_tags.include?("ActiveJob")  # <-- also crashes
end

  5. BroadcastLogger has no protection against corrupted formatters in its broadcasts. Its method_missing delegates blindly to all broadcasts that respond_to? a method, but doesn't account for the case where a broadcast said it could handle tagged (because TaggedLogging was mixed in at boot) but can no longer do so after a fork.

Two distinct crash points

Crash point 1: ActiveJob::Logging#logger_tagged_by_active_job? calls logger.formatter.current_tags on a Proc formatter.

Crash point 2: TaggedLogging#tagged calls formatter.tagged(...) on a Proc formatter. This is the one triggered via ActionCable/Turbo broadcasts.

Workaround

We use a 3-layer initializer:

# config/initializers/tagged_logging_fix.rb

# Repair any broadcast whose formatter lost TaggedLogging::Formatter
def repair_broadcast_logger_formatters(logger)
  return unless logger.is_a?(ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger)

  logger.broadcasts.each do |broadcast|
    next if broadcast.formatter.respond_to?(:current_tags)

    new_formatter = Logger::Formatter.new
    new_formatter.extend(ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging::Formatter)
    broadcast.formatter = new_formatter
  end
end

# Layer 1: Repair formatters at boot (covers Rails.logger and ActionCable)
Rails.application.config.after_initialize do
  repair_broadcast_logger_formatters(Rails.logger)
  repair_broadcast_logger_formatters(ActionCable.server.logger) if defined?(ActionCable)
end

# Layer 2: Guard ActiveJob's crash point
ActiveSupport.on_load(:active_job) do
  module ActiveJobTaggedLoggingFix
    private

    def logger_tagged_by_active_job?
      logger.formatter.respond_to?(:current_tags) &&
        logger.formatter.current_tags.include?("ActiveJob")
    end
  end

  prepend ActiveJobTaggedLoggingFix
end

# Layer 3: Make BroadcastLogger#tagged auto-repair on crash
# (catches post-fork corruption that Layer 1 can't prevent)
module BroadcastLoggerTaggedFix
  def tagged(*tags, &block)
    super
  rescue NoMethodError => e
    raise unless e.message.include?("tagged")

    repair_broadcast_logger_formatters(self)

    begin
      super
    rescue NoMethodError
      block ? yield : self
    end
  end
end

ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger.prepend(BroadcastLoggerTaggedFix)

We also construct the logger as a BroadcastLogger directly in production.rb to prevent Rails bootstrap from re-wrapping it:

# config/environments/production.rb
tagged_logger = ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging.logger(STDOUT)
config.logger = ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger.new(tagged_logger)

Suggested fix

A few things could be done in Rails itself:

  1. TaggedLogging#tagged should guard against corrupted formatters:

    def tagged(*tags)
  if block_given?
    if formatter.respond_to?(:tagged)
      formatter.tagged(*tags) { yield self }
    else
      yield self
    end
  # ...

  2. ActiveJob::Logging#logger_tagged_by_active_job? should guard:

    def logger_tagged_by_active_job?
  logger.formatter.respond_to?(:current_tags) &&
    logger.formatter.current_tags.include?("ActiveJob")
end

  3. BroadcastLogger could re-validate formatters after fork via an after_fork hook or by checking formatter health lazily on first use.

System configuration

Rails version: 8.1.3

Ruby version: 4.0.1

Other relevant gems: Puma 7.2.0, Solid Queue 1.4.0, Solid Cable 3.0.12, Turbo Rails 2.0.23

OS: macOS (Darwin 25.3.0, arm64) / Linux (Hetzner VPS, production)

Related issues

  • #49494 — BroadcastLogger as default logger in Rails 7.1 (closed, changelog request)
  • #51883 — BroadcastLogger + TaggedLogging TypeError (closed by stalebot, never fixed)
  • #49757 — BroadcastLogger#tagged without a block returns array (open)
items.title: BroadcastLogger formatters lose TaggedLogging extensions after fork (Puma + Solid Queue)

items.content_html:
Summary

At Shopify, we have been using different flavours of concurrency within ActiveJob for several years.
This year we have consolidated all of this functionality into one API method called concurrency.
After validating that this works for the scale of Shopify we decided to port the API upstream.

There have been others attempt to add locking to ActiveJob #33728

While that functionality has nothing wrong, we have identified that locking is not enough as a concurrency primitive.

At Shopify, we allow developers to specify multiple concurrency options for there jobs:

In all examples below, keys is the array of keys that will help build a unique concurrency key from the job arguments.

  • EndToEnd where a job holds a concurrency ticket from the moment gets enqueue until the job is performed. When any jobs that try to enter the queue, we check if the concurrent limit is reached, and if it is, we drop the job.
    concurrency(limit: 1, keys: ['checkout_id'])
class PaymentProcessingJob < ActiveJob
  # We only allow one job to be in the queue and processing at all times.
  # If a job tries to enter the queue while another job with the same checkout_id
  # is in the queue or performing, we drop the new job.

  # Do not want to charge the same checkout twice :)
  concurrency(limit: 1, keys: ['checkout_id'])

  def perform(params)
    # Logic
  end
end

  • EnqueueLimit where a job holds a concurrency ticket from the moment gets enqueue until the jobs get dequeued. When any jobs that try to enter the queue, we check if the concurrent limit is reached and if it is, we drop the job.
    concurrency(limit: { enqueue: 1 }, keys: ['checkout_id'])

  • PerformLimit where a job holds a concurrency ticket from the moment gets dequeued until the jobs get performed. At the time of the dequeue, we check if the concurrency limit is reached and if so we put that job back into the Delayed queue
    concurrency(limit: { performed: 1 }, keys: ['checkout_id'])

class UpdateThemeSettingsReferencesJob < ActiveJob
  # We only allow one job to perform at any moment. 
  # This is often used as a form of throttling for expensive operations.
  # When a job from the head of the queue tries to start performing while another job 
  # with the same key is already performing, we re-enqueue the new job with a delay.
  concurrency(
    limit: { perform: 1 },
    keys: ['shop_id', 'model', 'model_id']
  )

  def perform(params)
    # Logic 
  end
end
  • BoundedStages is the combination of EnqueueLimit and PerformLimit
    concurrency(limit: { enqueue: 1, perform:1 }, keys: ['checkout_id'])
class ExpensiveIdempotentSyncJob < ActiveJob
  # This job syncs the data of this shop with an external service.
  # Since it is expensive, we want only one sync running at a time for each shop.
  # We need to enqueue this job whenever something changes that requires syncing.
  # However, if there is already an ExpensiveSyncJob in the queue, that job will sync all the changes made
  # before it starts running, so there is no need to enqueue duplicates.
  concurrency(limit: { enqueue: 1, perform: 1 }, keys: ['shop_id'])

  def perform(params)
    # Logic 
  end
end

ActiveJob only care about the concurrency at the enqueue (EndToEnd and EnqueueLimit) steps for the perform cases (PerformLimit and BoundedStages) is up to the job adapters to implement it internally. So the adapters can decide to add the functionality or not 😄

Other Information

The timeout option allows specifying for how long a job can hold a concurrency ticket.

At Shopify, we allow other API options like perform_delay which configures the delay in which the job is placed back in the delayed queue when the PerformLimit is reached.

Here is an example of the API in use in one of our jobs:

concurrency(limit: { perform: 8, perform_delay: 300 }, keys: ['task_name'])
items.title: Add concurrency to ActiveJob

items.content_html:
ActiveJob#retry_on currently accepts Proc values for wait:, but it
rejects other Ruby callables such as Method objects and objects that
implement #call.

This change allows wait: to accept any callable object, while keeping
the existing behavior for proc-based wait handlers.

It also updates the retry_on API docs, adds tests for callable
objects and Method values, and documents the change in the Active Job
changelog.

Example:

class RetryDelay
  def call(executions, error)
    if error.message =~ /retry in (\d+)s/
      $1.to_i
    else
      executions * 2
    end
  end
end

class RemoteServiceJob < ActiveJob::Base
  retry_on CustomError, wait: RetryDelay.new
end

Testing:

AJ_ADAPTER=test bin/test activejob/test/cases/exceptions_test.rb
items.title: Allow retry_on wait to accept callable objects

items.content_html:
Steps to reproduce

In an app using Sidekiq enterprise with uniqueness:

# config/initializers/sidekiq.rb
[... other Sidekiq configuration? ...]
Sidekiq::Enterprise.unique! unless Rails.env.test?

# app/jobs/unique_job.rb
class UniqueJob < ApplicationJob
  sidekiq_options(unique_for: 30.minutes)

  def perform(params)
  end
end

Run two Rails consoles, one with the latest release ("old"), and one with main ("new"). First enqueue a unique job in "old", then in "new".

UniqueJob.perform_later((1..2))

Expected behavior

The job should enqueue successfully in "old", but the attempt to enqueue the job in "new" should print a log line like

INFO: Skipping enqueue for UniqueJob, not unique (lock held by JID 3b00cf8c382a9f4528c1325c)

Actual behavior

The job is successfully enqueued in both "old" and "new", violating the uniqueness constraint.

System configuration

Rails version: This is broken on main (8.1.0.beta1), but works on 8.0.2.1.

Ruby version: Tested on Ruby 3.4.4, but I don't think it matters much, so long as it's the same between both consoles.

Cause

The underlying cause is the optimization to AJ serialization in #55583 (commit 1f8a0c0). It changes the order of keys in the hash from

> ActiveJob::Arguments.serialize([(1..2)])
=> [{"_aj_serialized" => "ActiveJob::Serializers::RangeSerializer", "begin" => 1, "end" => 2, "exclude_end" => false}]

to

> ActiveJob::Arguments.serialize([(1..2)])
=> [{"begin" => 1, "end" => 2, "exclude_end" => false, "_aj_serialized" => "ActiveJob::Serializers::RangeSerializer"}]

This makes it appear that the two jobs use different arguments, as the serialized Hash is used to build a Redis key and these keys no longer match.
items.title: Active Job serialization optimizations break Sidekiq uniqueness

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #57148

logger_tagged_by_active_job? calls logger.formatter.current_tags unconditionally. When logger is a BroadcastLogger, formatter dispatches to the first broadcast's formatter. If that broadcast is a plain Logger (e.g. added by Solid Queue in-process mode), formatter is nil and the call raises NoMethodError.

The outer guard in tag_logger checks logger.respond_to?(:tagged), which returns true via BroadcastLogger#method_missing even when only a later broadcast responds — so the guard doesn't prevent the crash.

Reproduces without forking:

plain  = Logger.new(STDOUT)
tagged = ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging.new(Logger.new(STDOUT))
broadcast = ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger.new(plain, tagged)

broadcast.respond_to?(:tagged)    # => true
broadcast.formatter               # => nil
broadcast.formatter.current_tags  # => NoMethodError

Detail

Cache the formatter and guard with respond_to?. respond_to? is defined on NilClass (returns false), so it handles both nil and non-tagged formatters without &..

def logger_tagged_by_active_job?
  formatter = logger.formatter
  formatter.respond_to?(:current_tags) && formatter.current_tags.include?("ActiveJob")
end

Caching also avoids calling logger.formatter twice, which on BroadcastLogger dispatches through method_missing each time.

Additional information

Isolated logger_tagged_by_active_job? (Ruby 4.0.1):

Path Before After
Happy path (tagged first) 2.132M i/s 1.992M i/s (−7%)
Bug path (plain first, nil formatter) 741k i/s (rescue) 2.446M i/s (+3.3×)

The −7% on the happy path is one respond_to? call + local variable. The +3.3× on the bug path is the guard avoiding exception machinery.

Checklist

  • This Pull Request is related to one change. Unrelated changes should be opened in separate PRs.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: [Fix #issue-number]
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.
items.title: Fix NoMethodError in logger_tagged_by_active_job?

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Closes #52478

Prior to this commit, tests using assert_enqueued_with asserting against the at argument would incorrectly pass if testing with values that used second-level precision.

class BuggyJobTest < ActiveJob::TestCase
  def test_should_not_find_job
    at =  Time.new("1989-12-31T12:00:01")
    wait_until = Time.new("1989-12-31T12:00:02")

    assert_enqueued_with(job: BuggyJob, at:) do
      BuggyJob.set(wait_until:).perform_later
    end

    fail "Should not reach this line because assert_enqueued_with should have failed"
  end
end

Checklist

Before submitting the PR make sure the following are checked:

  • This Pull Request is related to one change. Unrelated changes should be opened in separate PRs.
  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. If this PR fixes a related issue include it in the commit message. Ex: [Fix #issue-number]
  • Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
  • CHANGELOG files are updated for the changed libraries if there is a behavior change or additional feature. Minor bug fixes and documentation changes should not be included.
items.title: Support second-level precision for `assert_enqueued_with`

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Working inside a large codebase I've noticed many tests which perform all enqueued jobs:

perform_enqueued_jobs do
  ...
end

For many tests performing all the enqueued jobs is overkill. For instance, I've come across tests which unnecessarily run an ElasticSearchIndexingJob along with the actual job being tested. This ends up slowing down the test suite with unrelated job runs.

This PR adds functionality allowing users to set a maximum number of 'side effects'. The maximum can be set locally as an argument inside perform_enqueued_jobs, for example:

# will raise ActiveJob::QueueAdapters::TestAdapter::MaximumSideEffectsReached
perform_enqueued_jobs(maximum_side_effects: 1) do
  assert_raises ActiveJob::QueueAdapters::TestAdapter::MaximumSideEffectsReached do
    HelloJob.perform_later
    GoodbyeJob.perform_later
  end
end

Or, the maximum number can be set globally for all tests, for example:

# will raise ActiveJob::QueueAdapters::TestAdapter::MaximumSideEffectsReached
ActiveJob::QueueAdapters::TestAdapter.maximum_side_effects = 1
  perform_enqueued_jobs do
    assert_raises ActiveJob::QueueAdapters::TestAdapter::MaximumSideEffectsReached do
      HelloJob.perform_later
      LoggingJob.perform_later
    end
end

When this threshold is breached, a MaximumSideEffectsReached error will be raised, encouraging users to specify which jobs to perform with the only: argument available to perform_enqueued_jobs:

"Maximum side effects threshold of #{threshold} reached. #{performed_jobs_count} jobs have already been performed. Consider using perform_enqueued_jobs with only: or except: or increase the threshold."

Detail

This Pull Request adds an optional class attribute to TestAdapter for global configuration and an optional argument to perform_enqueued_jobs for local configuration.

It then implements a counter to check the number of jobs performed against this threshold both on a block and block-less call to perform_enqueued_jobs.

I've added test coverage for each code path but welcome suggestions.

Additional information

In reworking tests on a large codebase, specifying which job to perform in calls to performed_enqueued_jobs shaved several seconds off individual tests. My hope is that by setting a threshold value for side effects other developers can identify unrelated jobs being performed in their tests and speed up their tests : )

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Adds a new :restart option to retry_job and retry_on for jobs
including ActiveJob::Continuable. By default, retried jobs resume from the last
saved checkpoint. In some cases, certain exceptions require restarting the job
from the beginning instead of resuming partially completed work.

This feature allows developers to selectively reset the job progress when needed,
while preserving the default behavior for normal continuable jobs.

It also ensures that internal continuation interrupts (Continuation::Interrupt)
still always resume from the last checkpoint, keeping the built-in semantics of
ActiveJob::Continuable unchanged.

Detail

  • Add restart option to retry_job:
    restart: false → resume from last saved checkpoint (default)
    restart: true → discard saved progress and start from the beginning
  • Updated retry_on to accept and pass the :restart option to retry_job.
  • Internal Continuation::Interrupt errors always force restart: false to maintain expected continuation flow and avoid resetting progress caused by normal pause or reschedule events.

Example usage:

class MyJob < ApplicationJob
  include ActiveJob::Continuable

  self.resume_errors_after_advancing = false
  retry_on RestartError, restart: true
  retry_on StandardError

  def perform(*args)
    step :step1 do
      # some step logic
    end

    step :step2 do
      # some step 2 logic that may cause RestartError
    end
  end
end

The :restart option can also be defined at the job level through resume_options,
allowing the job to fully restart on any StandardError.

Example usage:

class MyJob < ApplicationJob
  include ActiveJob::Continuable

  self.resume_options = { restart: true }

  def perform(*args)
    step :step1 do
      # some step logic
    end

    step :step2 do
      # some step 2 logic that may cause StandardError
    end
  end
end

Additional information

Although I was thinking — it might make sense to name the option for
resume_options (and the corresponding retry_job method) something like
:restart_on_exception, to make the behavior more explicit,
while keeping :restart for the retry_on method. Do you think that would be a better choice?

Motivation / Background

When using BroadcastLogger with multiple destinations, calling methods like tagged (which go through method_missing) would execute the provided block once for each destination logger. This caused problems in real-world usage - for
example, when using BroadcastLogger with ActiveJob, callbacks would fire multiple times instead of once.

The dispatch method already had logic to prevent this, but method_missing didn't apply the same safeguard.

Detail

This PR extracts the block-wrapping logic from dispatch into a new private method wrap_block_for_broadcast and applies it consistently in both dispatch and method_missing. The wrapper ensures blocks execute only once, with the
result cached and returned to subsequent loggers.

Changes:

  • Added wrap_block_for_broadcast helper method
  • Updated method_missing to wrap blocks before broadcasting
  • Added tests verifying blocks execute once regardless of destination count

Steps to reproduce

Run a job with retry attempt 1. The won't be retried.

class FooJob < ApplicationJob
  class FooError < StandardError; end

  retry_on FooError, attempts: 1

  def perform
    raise FooError
  end
end

Expected behavior

ActiveJob should retry at most the number of times specified by the attempts option.

Actual behavior

attempts: 0: runs once, no retry
attempts: 1: runs once, no retry
attempts: 2: runs once, one retry
attempts: 3: runs once, two retries

The behavior is not consistent. We can either change the behavior to be consistent (won't happen?) or at least document it very clearly.

#33816 also pointed out the problem.

Ruby version: ruby 3.1.1p18 (2022-02-18 revision 53f5fc4236) [x86_64-linux]

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

Fixes #55775

When a job mutates its arguments during execution and then retries, the mutated arguments are used for the retry instead of the original values. This can lead to unexpected behavior where retries operate on modified data.

Solution

This PR adds config.active_job.protect_retry_arguments (defaults to false for backward compatibility). When enabled, job arguments are deep-duplicated before execution, preventing mutations from affecting retries.

Steps to reproduce

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  gem "rails"
  # If you want to test against edge Rails replace the previous line with this:
  # gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "main"
end

require "active_job"
require "minitest/autorun"

class BuggyJob < ActiveJob::Base
  def perform
    puts "performed"
  end
end

class BuggyJobTest < ActiveJob::TestCase
  def test_should_not_find_job
    at =  Time.new("1989-12-31T12:00:01")
    wait_until = Time.new("1989-12-31T12:00:02")

    assert_raise ActiveSupport::TestCase::Assertion do
      assert_enqueued_with(job: BuggyJob, at:) do
        BuggyJob.set(wait_until:).perform_later
      end
    end
  end

  def test_assert_enqueued_with_date
    at = Date.tomorrow.noon
    wait_until = Date.tomorrow.noon

    assert_enqueued_with(job: BuggyJob, at:) do
      BuggyJob.set(wait_until:).perform_later
    end
  end

  def test_assert_enqueued_with_date_range
    at_matcher = ->(job_at) { (Date.yesterday..Date.tomorrow).cover?(job_at) }

    BuggyJob.set(wait_until: Date.today.noon).perform_later

    assert_enqueued_with(job: BuggyJob, at: at_matcher)
  end
end

Expected behavior

The test should fail, since the values are different.

Actual behavior

The test passes

items.content_html:
Motivation / Background

  • dependent: :destroy_async with an associated model that lacks a primary key fails in Ruby before enqueueing (e.g., TypeError: nil is not a symbol nor a string / to_sym on nil). We want a clear ActiveRecord error up front instead of a cryptic exception or later adapter error.
Minimal executable bug report (current main behavior) 
# bug_report_destroy_async_no_pk_main.rb
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"
  gem "rails", path: "."
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "active_job/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"
  config.active_job.queue_adapter = :test
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :owners_no_pk_async, force: true do |t|
    t.string :name
  end

  create_table :children_no_pk_async, id: false, force: true do |t|
    t.integer :owner_id
    t.string :name
  end
end

class OwnerNoPkAsync < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.table_name = "owners_no_pk_async"

  has_many :children_no_pk_async,
    class_name: "ChildNoPkAsync",
    foreign_key: :owner_id,
    dependent: :destroy_async
end

class ChildNoPkAsync < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.table_name = "children_no_pk_async"
  self.primary_key = nil

  belongs_to :owner_no_pk_async,
    class_name: "OwnerNoPkAsync",
    foreign_key: :owner_id
end

class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  class DummyDestroyJob < ActiveJob::Base
    queue_as :test
    def perform(*); end
  end

  def setup
    @previous_job = ActiveRecord::Base._destroy_association_async_job
    ActiveRecord::Base._destroy_association_async_job = DummyDestroyJob
  end

  def teardown
    ActiveRecord::Base._destroy_association_async_job = @previous_job if @previous_job
  end

  def test_destroy_async_on_no_pk_child_blows_up
    owner = OwnerNoPkAsync.create!(name: "owner")
    ChildNoPkAsync.create!(owner_no_pk_async: owner, name: "c1")
    error = assert_raises(TypeError) { owner.destroy }
    assert_match(/nil is not a symbol nor a string/, error.message)
  end
end
Post-fix version (raises UnknownPrimaryKey) 
# bug_report_destroy_async_no_pk_branch.rb
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"
  gem "rails", path: "."
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record/railtie"
require "active_job/railtie"
require "minitest/autorun"

ENV["DATABASE_URL"] = "sqlite3::memory:"

class TestApp < Rails::Application
  config.load_defaults Rails::VERSION::STRING.to_f
  config.eager_load = false
  config.logger = Logger.new($stdout)
  config.secret_key_base = "secret_key_base"
  config.active_job.queue_adapter = :test
end
Rails.application.initialize!

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :owners_no_pk_async, force: true do |t|
    t.string :name
  end

  create_table :children_no_pk_async, id: false, force: true do |t|
    t.integer :owner_id
    t.string :name
  end
end

class OwnerNoPkAsync < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.table_name = "owners_no_pk_async"

  has_many :children_no_pk_async,
    class_name: "ChildNoPkAsync",
    foreign_key: :owner_id,
    dependent: :destroy_async
end

class ChildNoPkAsync < ActiveRecord::Base
  self.table_name = "children_no_pk_async"
  self.primary_key = nil

  belongs_to :owner_no_pk_async,
    class_name: "OwnerNoPkAsync",
    foreign_key: :owner_id
end

class BugTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  class DummyDestroyJob < ActiveJob::Base
    queue_as :test
    def perform(*); end
  end

  def setup
    @previous_job = ActiveRecord::Base._destroy_association_async_job
    ActiveRecord::Base._destroy_association_async_job = DummyDestroyJob
  end

  def teardown
    ActiveRecord::Base._destroy_association_async_job = @previous_job if @previous_job
  end

  def test_destroy_async_on_no_pk_child_raises_unknown_primary_key
    owner = OwnerNoPkAsync.create!(name: "owner")
    ChildNoPkAsync.create!(owner_no_pk_async: owner, name: "c1")

    error = assert_raises(ActiveRecord::UnknownPrimaryKey) { owner.destroy }
    assert_includes error.message, "cannot destroy associated records asynchronously without a primary key"
  end
end

Detail

  • Add an early guard in has_many and has_one dependent: :destroy_async to raise ActiveRecord::UnknownPrimaryKey when the associated model lacks a primary key, before enqueueing jobs.

Additional information

  • No semantic change for valid setups; only broken no-PK associations now fail earlier with a clear error instead of a cryptic exception.
  • Test added: activerecord/test/cases/associations/destroy_async_no_primary_key_test.rb (covers has_many/has_one).

  • Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why.
  • Tests are added or updated.
  • CHANGELOG not updated (bug fix / DX improvement).

items.content_html:
Steps to reproduce

ActiveJob::TestHelper recomputes queue_adapter_changed_jobs in both before_setup and after_teardown:

def before_setup
  queue_adapter_specific_to_this_test_class = queue_adapter_for_test
  queue_adapter_changed_jobs.each do |klass|
    # ...
  end
  # ...
end

def after_teardown
  super
  queue_adapter_changed_jobs.each { |klass| klass.disable_test_adapter }
end

def queue_adapter_changed_jobs
  (ActiveJob::Base.descendants << ActiveJob::Base).select do |klass|
    # only override explicitly set adapters, a quirk of `class_attribute`
    klass.singleton_class.public_instance_methods(false).include?(:_queue_adapter)
  end
end

That makes every test that includes ActiveJob::TestHelper pay an O(number_of_job_classes) scan twice per test, even when the test does not enqueue jobs and even when no job-specific queue adapter changed.

Here is a small benchmark that mirrors a large Rails app with many job classes:

# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"
  gem "activejob", "8.1.3"
  gem "benchmark-ips"
end

require "active_job"
require "active_job/test_helper"
require "benchmark/ips"

class ApplicationJob < ActiveJob::Base; end

2_500.times do |i|
  Object.const_set("GeneratedJob#{i}", Class.new(ApplicationJob))
end

helper = Object.new.extend(ActiveJob::TestHelper)

puts "ActiveJob #{ActiveJob::VERSION::STRING}"
puts "Job descendants: #{ActiveJob::Base.descendants.size}"
puts "Changed jobs: #{helper.send(:queue_adapter_changed_jobs).size}"

Benchmark.ips do |x|
  x.config(time: 5, warmup: 2)

  x.report("queue_adapter_changed_jobs") do
    helper.send(:queue_adapter_changed_jobs)
  end

  x.report("[ActiveJob::Base]") do
    [ActiveJob::Base]
  end

  x.compare!
end

On my machine this produces:

ActiveJob 8.1.3
Job descendants: 2501
Changed jobs: 1
ruby 4.0.5 (2026-05-20 revision 64336ffd0e) +PRISM [arm64-darwin24]

queue_adapter_changed_jobs    762.293 i/s    (1.31 ms/i)
[ActiveJob::Base]              21.772M i/s   (45.93 ns/i)

Because queue_adapter_changed_jobs runs in both setup and teardown, this benchmark translates to about 2.6 ms of reflection overhead per test at this scale. In a large Rails app, this method shows up prominently in test-suite profiles; the hot operation is Module#public_instance_methods(false), which allocates an array for each job class and then linearly scans it.

Expected behavior

Changing / resetting Active Job's test queue adapter should not require a full reflection scan of every ActiveJob::Base descendant before and after every test.

Ideally the work should be proportional to the number of jobs that actually have an explicitly changed adapter, or avoided entirely for tests that do not need Active Job test adapter setup.

Actual behavior

Every test that includes ActiveJob::TestHelper pays the descendant scan twice:

  1. once in before_setup, to enable the test adapter; and
  2. once in after_teardown, to disable it.

This is especially expensive in large applications where:

  • there may be thousands of ActiveJob::Base descendants;
  • ActiveJob::TestHelper can be included by broad test base classes or indirectly through mailer test helpers;
  • most tests do not enqueue jobs; and
  • the set of classes with explicit queue adapters is usually tiny and stable after boot.

Possible directions

A few possible ways to avoid the per-test full scan:

  • Track classes when queue_adapter= / _queue_adapter= is explicitly assigned, and have queue_adapter_changed_jobs read that tracked set instead of reflecting over all descendants.
  • Cache the result when classes are eager-loaded, with an invalidation path for lazy loading / reloading / newly defined test jobs.
  • Lazily install the test adapter only around helper operations that need it instead of in every test setup.
  • If current class_attribute inheritance semantics mean setting the test adapter on ActiveJob::Base is sufficient, consider avoiding the descendant scan and operating on ActiveJob::Base directly.

I am happy to work on a PR, but wanted to confirm the preferred direction first because this code has some subtle compatibility history around per-job queue adapters in tests.

System configuration

Rails version: Active Job / Active Support 8.1.3; the same implementation exists on rails/rails main / 8.2.0.alpha

Ruby version: ruby 4.0.5
items.title: ActiveJob::TestHelper scans all job descendants twice per test to reset queue adapters
